notes: APC (Siaka Stevens, PM since April 1968) in ruling slot 3 with its MD sprite. SLPP stays in MD slot 2. Coalition slot 18 has no real 1970 partner (APC governs alone); filled with the Forna-Taqi radical wing of the APC, which broke away in Sept 1970. Sierra Leone is still a Commonwealth realm until April 1971, so slot 23 = House of Windsor. UDP (founded Sept 1970) deliberately omitted.

0.name: The Margai Machine
0.text:
The Margai Machine is the network of Sir Albert Margai, Prime Minister from 1964 to 1967, who tried to turn Sierra Leone into an SLPP one-party state before losing the 1967 election. On 1 January 1970 Margai lives abroad, but his loyal chiefs, financiers and officers still dream of a return.

It stands for strong executive rule, Mende-led patronage, close ties to Britain and the West and hostility to Stevens' radicals. Its base is southern and eastern chiefs, wealthy SLPP backers and sympathizers in the officer corps, and its leverage lies in money and the bitterness of the south after 1967.

1.name: United Progressive Party
1.text:
The UPP was founded in 1954 by the Freetown lawyer Cyril Rogers-Wright as a party of the Krio community of the Western Area. It won seats in the early elections but has since shrunk to a Freetown rump; on 1 January 1970 its members drift between the APC and independent politics.

It defends the rule of law, the professions, property rights, Christian education and a parliamentary constitution on the British model, wary of both chiefly rule and populist radicalism. Its base is Krio lawyers, clergy, teachers and merchants, and its leverage lies in their weight in the courts, the press and the civil service.

2.name: Sierra Leone People's Party
2.text:
The SLPP led Sierra Leone to independence in 1961 under Sir Milton Margai and governed until the disputed 1967 election and the coups that followed. On 1 January 1970 it is the parliamentary opposition, weakened by election petitions, defections and harassment, led in the House by Salia Jusu-Sheriff.

It stands for gradual development, a market economy with foreign investment, a pro-Western foreign policy and partnership between the chiefs and the educated elite. Its base is the Mende south and east and the paramount chiefs, and its leverage lies in its strong rural network and its claim to be the party of independence.

3.name: All People's Congress
3.text:
The APC was founded in 1960 by the trade unionist Siaka Stevens and won the 1967 election, taking office in April 1968 after the military interlude. On 1 January 1970 Stevens is Prime Minister, ruling with a mix of populist reform and growing pressure on the opposition.

It speaks for workers, the urban poor and the north against the chiefly and Mende establishment, promising state control of diamonds, Africanization and a more independent foreign policy. Its base is the Temne and Limba north, Freetown's youth and the unions, and its leverage lies in government patronage and its mass street support.

4.name: Heirs of Wallace-Johnson
4.text:
I. T. A. Wallace-Johnson, founder of the West African Youth League in 1938 and the country's pioneering Marxist agitator, died in 1965. On 1 January 1970 his heirs are a scattering of old unionists, journalists and Soviet-educated graduates who meet in Freetown study circles.

They want a workers' party on the Leninist model, nationalization of the mines and banks, and an alliance with Moscow and Conakry against British capital. Their base is a few union branches, teachers and returning students from the Eastern bloc, and their leverage lies in their influence on the left wing of the APC.

5.name: The Fourah Bay Radicals
5.text:
Fourah Bay College on Mount Aureol, the oldest Western-style university in West Africa, has become a centre of student radicalism. On 1 January 1970 its activists read Fanon, Nkrumah and Che Guevara and organize protests against corruption, the chiefs and foreign companies.

They demand a revolutionary break with neo-colonialism, Black Power solidarity with the diaspora, free education and an end to elite privilege. Their base is students, young lecturers and unemployed school-leavers in Freetown, and their leverage lies in demonstrations and the press, which can embarrass any government.

6.name: The Conakry Axis
6.text:
The Conakry Axis is the hardline wing of the northern political class that looks to Sékou Touré's Guinea as a model and protector. On 1 January 1970 its members sit in APC committees and the security services and urge Stevens to seek Guinean backing against coups and the SLPP.

They stand for a one-party state, a mutual defence pact with Guinea, close ties to the Eastern bloc and suspicion of Britain and the Western mining companies. Their base is northern party bosses and cross-border Temne and Susu networks, and their leverage lies in Guinean money, militia and the fear of another army coup.

7.name: Special Branch
7.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence wing of the Sierra Leone Police, inherited from the colonial administration. On 1 January 1970 it watches the SLPP opposition, disgruntled officers and student radicals for the Stevens government.

Its senior officers favour a strong state, preventive detention and states of emergency over parliamentary niceties, and are willing to serve whoever holds power. Its base is police intelligence officers and informers in every district, and its leverage lies in its files, its ability to make arrests and its role in uncovering coup plots.

8.name: Musa Sadr's Freetown Followers
8.text:
Sierra Leone's Lebanese community, many of them Shia from southern Lebanon, dominates retail trade and the diamond business from Freetown to Kenema. On 1 January 1970 its religious leaders look to Imam Musa al-Sadr, whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut was founded in 1969.

They favour a socially engaged Shia Islam that builds schools and charities, protects the community and avoids open politics. Their base is merchants, diamond dealers and their families, and their leverage lies in their economic weight and the credit they extend to politicians of every party.

9.name: The Najaf Circle
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small group of young Lebanese Shia from Sierra Leone who have studied in the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini teaches. On 1 January 1970 they preach piety and political awareness in the community's prayer halls.

They reject secular nationalism and Western influence and want clerics to guide the community in public affairs. Their base is devout youth and a few wealthy patrons, and their leverage lies in diaspora remittances and the seminary links that bind Freetown to Iraq and southern Lebanon.

10.name: Sierra Leone Muslim Congress
10.text:
The Sierra Leone Muslim Congress is the country's long-established association of Muslim notables, founded under colonial rule to represent the community before the government. On 1 January 1970 it speaks for imams, alkalis and Muslim traders in a country where Muslims are a majority but Christians dominate the elite.

It seeks government support for mosques, Arabic and Islamic schools, pilgrimage arrangements and Muslim representation in public life, and is cautious and loyal to established authority. Its base is the Muslim quarters of Freetown and provincial towns, and its leverage lies in delivering the votes of the faithful.

11.name: Northern Wahhabiyya
11.text:
In the trading towns of the north, from Kabala to Kambia, pilgrims and graduates of Arab schools preach the strict reformism West Africans call Wahhabiyya. On 1 January 1970 they are a small minority, disputing with Sufi brotherhoods and the established imams.

They condemn saint veneration, secret societies and secular politics, and call for a society governed by the Sharia. Their base is young traders and Fula and Mandinka merchants with ties to Guinea and Mecca, and their leverage lies in trade networks, private Quranic schools and frustration with the corruption of politicians.

12.name: Fourah Bay Jamaat
12.text:
Fourah Bay and Fula Town are the old Muslim Aku quarters of Freetown, home of the city's Yoruba-descended Muslims and their historic mosques. On 1 January 1970 a circle of educated reformers there seeks to modernize Muslim life and compete with Christian mission schools.

They promote Muslim secondary schools, Arabic and English education, social welfare and moral renewal in politics, drawing on Egyptian reform thought. Their base is Krio Muslim professionals, teachers and traders, and their leverage lies in their education, their mosque associations and their access to Freetown's political class.

13.name: The Tower Hill Mandarins
13.text:
Tower Hill, above Freetown, is the seat of Parliament and government, and its mandarins are the permanent secretaries and senior administrators who outlasted Margai, the juntas and the return of civilian rule. On 1 January 1970 they serve Stevens while guarding their own continuity.

They favour orderly, centralized administration, technocratic planning and a non-partisan state that keeps foreign donors and mining companies satisfied. Their base is the senior civil service and the provincial secretaries, and their leverage lies in the fact that no government can run without them.

14.name: The Paramount Chiefs' Bench
14.text:
Sierra Leone's paramount chiefs rule its chiefdoms under customary law and send their own members to the House of Representatives. On 1 January 1970 many chiefs who backed the SLPP fear removal by the new APC government, while others hurry to make peace with Stevens.

They stand for customary land tenure, the authority of the chiefdom councils and secret societies, local taxation and a share in mining royalties. Their base is the rural chiefdoms across the provinces, and their leverage lies in their control of land, labour and votes in the countryside.

15.name: Sierra Leone Selection Trust
15.text:
The SLST, a British mining company linked to Consolidated African Selection Trust, has held the main diamond concessions in Kono since the 1930s. On 1 January 1970 it remains the country's largest earner of foreign exchange, while the government prepares to take a majority stake.

It wants secure concessions, low taxes and protection against illicit diggers and smugglers, and works through quiet deals with whichever government is in power. Its base is shareholders in London, expatriate managers and the officials who depend on its revenue, and its leverage lies in its control of the diamond economy.

16.name: The Koidu Diamond Dealers
16.text:
Koidu in Kono District is the boom town of alluvial diamonds, where licensed dealers, Lebanese and Mandinka traders and thousands of diggers buy and sell outside the SLST fences. On 1 January 1970 they operate in a grey zone between legal licences and smuggling to Liberia.

They want open digging licences, low duties, free trade in stones and no state monopoly over marketing. Their base is dealers, tributors and diggers in the diamond districts, and their leverage lies in the cash they move and the politicians they finance.

17.name: Friends of the Gola Forest
17.text:
The Gola Forest reserves along the Liberian border hold the last great lowland rainforest of Sierra Leone. On 1 January 1970 a handful of forestry officers, Njala agronomists and naturalists warn that logging, farming and diamond pits are destroying the country's forests and rivers.

They call for protected reserves, reforestation, controls on mining spoil and sustainable rice farming. Their base is the forestry department, teachers and a few chiefs in the reserve areas, and their leverage lies in international scientific interest and the threat that erosion poses to farmland.

18.name: Forna–Taqi Wing
18.text:
The Forna–Taqi Wing is the radical tendency inside the APC around Finance Minister Mohamed Sorie Forna and Ibrahim Taqi, both prominent in the party's founding generation. On 1 January 1970 they sit in Stevens' cabinet, impatient with his compromises and his growing personal power.

They want faster nationalization of the diamond industry, land and social reform, curbs on the chiefs and a non-aligned, anti-colonial foreign policy. Their base is northern intellectuals, younger party cadres and union activists, and their leverage lies in their ministerial posts and their standing with the party's radical wing.

19.name: The Little Red Book Circle
19.text:
Chinese literature and the quotations of Mao Zedong circulate among Freetown's student radicals and young teachers, and a small circle has embraced them. On 1 January 1970 they meet informally, contemptuous of both British capital and Soviet revisionism.

They preach rural revolution, self-reliance, peasant mobilization against the chiefs and solidarity with liberation movements in Guinea-Bissau. Their base is a few students, teachers and unemployed graduates, and their leverage lies only in pamphlets, campus debates and their contacts with China's growing presence in West Africa.

20.name: Sons of the Protectorate
20.text:
The Sons of the Protectorate carry the old grievance of the provinces against the Krio elite of the former Colony, who long dominated education, the professions and the civil service. On 1 January 1970 their rhetoric runs through rallies of both major parties.

They demand jobs, scholarships and promotions for 'sons of the soil', limits on Lebanese and foreign traders and a government that answers to the provinces rather than Freetown. Their base is provincial youth, petty traders and local politicians, and their leverage lies in mobilizing resentment at election time.

21.name: Juxon-Smith Loyalists
21.text:
The loyalists are officers and officials who served Brigadier Andrew Juxon-Smith's National Reformation Council, the junta that ruled from 1967 until the sergeants' coup of April 1968. On 1 January 1970 Juxon-Smith is a prisoner of the new government, and his followers are purged or watched.

They believe civilian politicians are corrupt and tribal, and that only disciplined military rule can clean up the state and the economy. Their base is a dwindling group of former junta officers and sympathizers, and their leverage lies in grudges inside the army.

22.name: Royal Sierra Leone Military Forces
22.text:
The Royal Sierra Leone Military Forces grew out of the colonial Royal West African Frontier Force and staged two coups in 1967 and 1968. On 1 January 1970 Brigadier John Bangura, restored by the April 1968 counter-coup, commands the army.

Its officers value professional autonomy and a voice in national affairs, distrusting both SLPP and APC patronage. Their base is the Wilberforce barracks and the officer corps, and their leverage lies in being the only force that can make or break governments, as it has already done twice.
22.wiki: Republic of Sierra Leone Armed Forces

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
Sierra Leone has been a Commonwealth realm since independence in 1961, and Queen Elizabeth II remains its head of state on 1 January 1970, represented by Acting Governor-General Banja Tejan-Sie. The APC government openly plans to make the country a republic.

Supporters of the crown value the link to Britain, the Commonwealth and an apolitical head of state above party rivalries. Their base is Krio professionals, the judiciary, older civil servants and SLPP moderates, and their leverage lies in constitutional procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority to abolish the monarchy.
